t: Make Array Zero by Subtracting Equal Amounts — Distinct Values Count
o: Subtracting x from all positive elements preserves their relative differences, so effectively each operation 'eliminates' one distinct positive value level: choosing x equal to the current minimum zeroes exactly the elements at that level. Hence the answer is the number of distinct nonzero values. Example [1,5,0,3,5] has distinct positives {1,3,5} → 3 operations; [0] → 0.
k: Each operation removes one distinct positive value tier, so the count of distinct nonzero elements is optimal.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Set of Nonzero Values
a.i: Insert all nonzero elements into a set; its size is the answer. Alternatively sort and count value changes — identical complexity here.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with hash inserts.
a.sp: O(n) for the set (or O(1) with a 101-bit bitmap).

a.i: Sorting groups equal values together; the number of distinct positive values equals the count of positions where the value increases past zero. Avoids hashing and uses O(1) extra space if sorting in place.
s: Count indices i where nums[i] > 0 and (i == 0 or nums[i] > nums[i-1]).

w: Either approach is fine; the set version is one line. Pitfall: zeros must not be counted. Follow-up: if x must be chosen adversarially or subtraction applies to a subrange, the problem becomes harder (segment-tree beats territory).
